q: Which hook gives a function component state that triggers a re-render when it changes?
why: useState stores a value and re-renders the component whenever its setter is called. useRef also persists values, but changing it does NOT re-render.

q: What does this print?
why: A famous JavaScript quirk: typeof null is "object" (a legacy bug), while typeof undefined is "undefined".

q: The number on this button never changes when clicked. Why?
options: count++ is not valid inside JSX
Changing a plain variable doesn't trigger a re-render — it needs useState
why: React only re-renders when state or props change. Use const [count, setCount] = useState(0) and call setCount(count + 1).

q: Your landing page scores badly because a 3 MB hero image blocks loading. What's the best FIRST fix?
options: Serve a compressed, responsive image (WebP + srcset) and lazy-load the rest
Rewrite the page as a class component
Inline the image as base64 inside the CSS
why: Oversized images are the #1 cause of slow loading. Compress, serve the right size and lazy-load what isn't visible yet. Base64 inlining makes the CSS even heavier.

q: With the default box-sizing, how wide does this box render on screen?
why: content-box adds padding and border on top of width: 200 + 20×2 + 5×2 = 250px. With box-sizing: border-box it would stay 200px.

q: Which Spring annotation turns a class into a controller whose methods return JSON bodies?
why: @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody, so every method's return value is written straight to the HTTP response (as JSON by default).

q: What does this Java code print?
why: == compares object references (a is from the string pool, b is a new object) → false. equals() compares the characters → true.

q: What is wrong with this endpoint's design?
options: Creating a resource should use @PostMapping, not GET
why: GET must be safe and read-only. Creating data belongs to POST (returning 201 Created). GET requests can also be cached or retried by browsers and proxies.

q: One client is hitting your API 1,000 times per second and the database is slowing down for everyone. What's the best first protection?
options: Rate limiting per client (e.g. token bucket)
why: Rate limiting caps each client's requests so one noisy caller can't starve others. Caching and DB indexing help too, but limiting is the first guard.

q: Which HTTP status code best fits “the resource was created successfully”?
why: 201 Created tells the client a new resource now exists (usually with a Location header pointing to it).

q: Which SQL clause filters groups AFTER a GROUP BY has been applied?
why: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups created by GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates like COUNT(*).

q: The orders table has amounts 100, NULL and 250. What does this query return?
why: COUNT(*) counts rows (3). COUNT(column) skips NULL values, so COUNT(amount) is 2.

q: Why does this query fail in strict SQL mode?
options: name is neither aggregated nor in a GROUP BY — it needs GROUP BY name
why: Mixing a plain column with an aggregate requires GROUP BY on that column, otherwise the database doesn't know which name to show.

q: A report query on a 10-million-row table filters by email and takes 12 seconds. What's the best first fix?
options: Add an index on the email column
Split it into 10 million small queries
why: An index on email lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.

q: Which JOIN keeps ALL rows from the left table, even when there's no match on the right?
why: LEFT JOIN returns every left-table row and fills right-table columns with NULL when nothing matches.

q: What is the main purpose of the key prop when you render a list in React?
options: To help React identify which items were added, removed or changed
why: Stable keys let React match old and new items so it updates only what changed. Without them (or with array indexes on reorderable lists) React can re-render too much or mix up state.

q: What does this print?
why: Numbers use binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not exactly 0.3. Compare with a small tolerance instead.

q: This component keeps calling the API in an endless loop. What is the fix?
options: Add an empty dependency array [] so the effect runs only once after mount
Call fetch directly inside the JSX
Wrap the component in a div
why: An effect with no dependency array runs after EVERY render. Each fetch sets state, which re-renders, which fetches again. [] runs it once (add values to the array if the effect depends on them).

q: A search box calls your API on every keystroke and the server is overloaded. What is the best fix?
options: Debounce the input so the request fires only after the user pauses typing
Call the API twice to be safe
Move the input outside the form
why: Debouncing waits (e.g. 300 ms) after the last keystroke before calling the API, which cuts requests dramatically without hurting the experience.

q: Which CSS centres a child both horizontally and vertically inside a flex container that has a height?
why: On a flex container, justify-content centres along the main axis and align-items along the cross axis. The container needs a height for vertical centring to be visible.

q: What does BCrypt do that a plain SHA-256 hash of a password does not?
options: It is deliberately slow and adds a random salt, so brute-force and rainbow-table attacks are much harder
It encrypts the password so you can decrypt it later
It sends the password over HTTPS
why: Fast hashes let attackers try billions of guesses per second. BCrypt is intentionally slow, salted per password, and one-way - you can only verify a guess, never decrypt.

q: What is Dependency Injection in Spring?
options: The framework creates objects and hands them to the classes that need them, instead of those classes calling new
A way to make the build faster
why: Spring builds your beans and passes them in (usually through the constructor). Classes depend on interfaces, which makes code loosely coupled and easy to test with fakes.

q: What is the biggest problem with this code?
code:
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'";
statement.executeQuery(sql);
options: It is vulnerable to SQL injection - use a PreparedStatement with parameters
Strings cannot be joined with + in Java
why: A name like ' OR '1'='1 changes the query itself. Parameterised queries (PreparedStatement, JPA named parameters) send data separately, so input can never become SQL.

q: Two users apply for the last open slot at the same moment and both succeed, so the numbers go wrong. What helps most?
options: A transaction with locking - for example a unique constraint or an optimistic lock (@Version)
why: This is a race condition. Let the database enforce the rule: a unique constraint, a row lock, or optimistic locking makes the second request fail cleanly instead of corrupting data.

q: What happens when this code runs?
options: It throws UnsupportedOperationException because List.of() is immutable
why: List.of() returns an unmodifiable list. Use new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)) when you need to add elements.

q: Which window function lets you keep exactly one row per customer (for example the latest one) when removing duplicates?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY signup_date DESC)
why: Number the rows inside each customer group and keep row 1. LIMIT 1 would return one row for the whole table, not one per customer.

q: What does this query return?
why: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument - here the third value, 'N/A'.

q: This query returns no rows even though some orders have no customer. Why?
code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = NULL;
options: = NULL is never true - NULL must be tested with IS NULL
NULL must be written in quotes
SELECT * cannot be combined with WHERE
why: NULL means unknown, so comparing it with = always gives unknown (not true). Use WHERE customer_id IS NULL.

q: Your dashboard needs total sales per month. Which query shape is right?
options: GROUP BY the month of the order date and SUM(amount)
why: Grouping by month collapses all orders of a month into one row, and SUM adds their amounts.

q: A teammate ran UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled'; without a WHERE and every order changed. What should you do before risky UPDATE or DELETE statements?
options: Run it inside a transaction (or test it with a SELECT first) so you can check the result and ROLLBACK
why: A transaction lets you inspect the affected rows and roll back mistakes. Previewing with a SELECT that uses the same WHERE catches most errors.

q: Your model scores 99% on the training data but only 70% on new data. What is this problem called?
why: The model memorised the training data (including its noise) instead of learning patterns that generalise to new data.

q: What does this Python code print?
code:
preds = [1 if s > 0.5 else 0 for s in [0.2, 0.9, 0.6]]
print(preds)
why: 0.2 is not above 0.5 so it becomes 0; 0.9 and 0.6 are above 0.5 so both become 1.

q: What is wrong with the order of these two lines?
options: fit_transform cannot be used on arrays
train_test_split must run before importing sklearn
Nothing is wrong. Scaling before splitting is the recommended way
The scaler learns from the test data too (data leakage). Split first, then fit the scaler on the training part only
why: Fitting the scaler on all rows lets information from the test set leak into training, so the test score looks better than it really is.

q: A fraud dataset has 99% normal and 1% fraud transactions. Your model predicts "normal" every time. What accuracy does it get and what is the problem?
options: 99% accuracy, but it catches no fraud. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data
99% accuracy and it is a great model
why: With imbalanced classes, accuracy hides the failure. Look at recall, precision or F1 for the rare class instead.

q: Which metric matters most when missing a real positive case is very costly (for example, disease screening)?
why: Recall = real positives found / all real positives. High recall means few real cases are missed.

q: What does this Python code print?
why: b = a does not copy the list. Both names point to the same list, so appending through b changes a too.

q: What does a learning rate that is too high usually cause in gradient descent?
options: The loss can bounce around or diverge because each step overshoots the minimum
Training always finishes faster with a better result
why: Big steps jump over the lowest point. A smaller learning rate takes steadier steps.

q: Your regression model has a high error on both the training data and the test data. What is the most likely issue?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the data
why: If even the training error is high, the model cannot capture the pattern. Try better features or a more flexible model.

q: Why is this evaluation wrong?
options: accuracy_score only works on training data
predict() must be called on X_train
The print statement is not allowed
Predictions for the test set are compared with the training labels. It should use y_test
why: Predictions must be compared with the true labels of the same rows, so y_test goes with X_test.

q: Which technique turns a category like "red", "green", "blue" into numbers without implying any order?
why: One-hot encoding makes one 0/1 column per category, so the model does not think blue > red.

q: 5-fold cross-validation gives accuracies 0.91, 0.90, 0.92, 0.55, 0.91. What should you do?
options: Investigate the odd fold (unshuffled or unusual data?) before trusting the average
why: One very different fold is a warning sign of how the data was split or of a data problem. Find the cause first.

q: Why do we keep a separate test set that the model never trains on?
options: To measure how the model performs on data it has not seen
To increase the number of features
why: Only unseen data shows whether the model generalises. Scores on training data are too optimistic.

q: What is the main benefit of a Docker container compared with installing an app directly on a server?
options: It makes the app run faster than native code
It removes the need for an operating system
The app runs with its own dependencies in an isolated, repeatable package
why: "It works on my machine" problems shrink because the container carries the app and everything it needs.

q: What does this shell script print?
code:
x=5
if [ $x -gt 3 ]; then echo big; else echo small; fi
options: Nothing, it is a syntax error
why: -gt means "greater than". 5 is greater than 3, so the first branch runs.

q: Why is this Dockerfile slow to rebuild after every small code change?
code:
FROM node:20
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
options: Copying all the source before npm install invalidates the cached install layer on every change. Copy package.json first
CMD must be written before FROM
RUN is not allowed in a Dockerfile
why: Docker caches each layer. Copy package*.json, run npm install, and only then copy the rest, so dependencies are reinstalled only when they change.

q: A new deployment broke production five minutes ago. What is the best first action?
options: Edit the code directly on the production server
Wait to see if it fixes itself
Roll back to the last working version, then investigate
Delete the logs to save space
why: Restore service first, then find the cause calmly with the logs. Fixing live on the server is risky.

q: What does CI (Continuous Integration) mean?
options: Deploying to production once a year
Manually copying files to the server
Every code change is automatically built and tested, many times a day
Backing up the database every night
why: CI catches broken code early because each change is merged and tested automatically.

q: What is "Infrastructure as Code" (for example Terraform)?
options: Describing servers and networks in versioned files so they can be created repeatably
Writing code that only runs on physical servers
why: Because the setup is in files, you can review it, version it in Git and recreate the same environment any time.

q: What does this command print?
why: cut splits the text at commas (-d) and -f2 picks the second field, which is b.

q: Your server disk is 100% full and the app is crashing. Which command helps you find the folders using the most space?
why: du ("disk usage") shows how much space each folder uses. ping tests the network and chmod changes permissions.

q: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
options: A container shares the host OS kernel and is lighter. A VM includes a full guest operating system
A container needs a full OS each. A VM does not
They are exactly the same thing
VMs always start faster than containers
why: Sharing the kernel makes containers small and quick to start. VMs are heavier but isolate more strongly.

q: What is the security problem here?
options: A secret is committed to the repository. Use environment secrets or a secrets manager instead
environment cannot be used in a compose file
why: Anyone who can read the repo can read the password, and it stays in the Git history. Keep secrets out of code.

q: You want to release a new version with no downtime. Which approach helps?
options: Stop the app, deploy, and start it again at night
Deploy straight to the only server and hope
Rolling or blue-green deployment: start the new version, move traffic over, then stop the old one
why: Running old and new side by side lets traffic shift smoothly, and you can switch back if something is wrong.

q: What does a health check (liveness / readiness probe) do?
options: It measures how many users signed up
It lets the platform detect an unhealthy app and restart it or stop sending traffic to it
why: Probes let Kubernetes or a load balancer react automatically when an instance stops responding.

q: Why should network calls NOT run on the main (UI) thread of a mobile app?
options: They can freeze the screen, and the OS may show "App not responding" or close the app
Mobile networks only work for background apps
The UI thread has no internet permission
It makes the battery charge faster
why: The main thread draws the screen and handles touches. If it waits for the network, the app looks frozen.

q: What does this Kotlin code print?
code:
val list = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4)
println(list.filter { it % 2 == 0 }.map { it * 10 })
why: filter keeps the even numbers (2 and 4), then map multiplies each by 10.

q: Why does the counter on screen never change?
code:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
const add = () => { count = count + 1; };
options: State must be changed with setCount(). Assigning to count does not update the screen (and a const cannot be reassigned)
add must be an async function
why: The setter tells React to re-render. Writing to the variable directly does nothing visible.

q: Users on slow, unreliable networks see a blank feed screen. What is a good improvement?
options: Force users to switch to Wi-Fi
Cache the last data locally and show it immediately, then refresh in the background with clear loading and error states
why: Showing saved content first makes the app feel fast and useful even on a bad connection.

q: What does the app lifecycle mean for your code?
options: Apps always run until the user closes them
Only the developer decides when the app stops
The lifecycle only matters on tablets
The OS can pause, stop or kill your screen at any time, so you must save state and release resources
why: Because the system can reclaim memory, important data must be saved when the screen goes to the background.

q: Why do apps ask for permissions (camera, location) at runtime?
options: The user stays in control of their privacy, so the app should explain why it needs it and cope if the answer is no
Permissions are only needed for games
Stores require every app to ask for every permission
why: Ask only for what you need, at the moment you need it, and handle a refusal politely.

q: A list of 5,000 items scrolls slowly and uses a lot of memory. Which approach helps most?
options: Use a lazy / recycling list (RecyclerView, LazyColumn, FlatList) that creates only the visible rows
why: Recycling lists reuse a few row views as you scroll, which keeps memory and work small.

q: What does this Dart code print?
why: b is [2, 4, 6] so its length is 3. a.first is 1. 3 + 1 = 4.

q: What is the difference between a native app and a cross-platform app (Flutter, React Native)?
options: Native apps cannot use the camera
Native apps are written separately for each platform. Cross-platform apps share most code between Android and iOS
Cross-platform apps only run in the browser
why: Cross-platform saves effort by sharing code. Native gives the deepest access to each platform.

q: Where should an app store a login token securely?
options: In a public text file on the SD card
In the platform secure storage (Android Keystore / EncryptedSharedPreferences, iOS Keychain)
why: Secure storage encrypts the value with keys protected by the device, so other apps cannot read it.

q: What is wrong with this Kotlin code, called from onCreate()?
options: A blocking network call runs on the main thread. Move it to a coroutine or background thread
why: Do the slow work in the background, then update the screen with the result.

q: What is a responsive layout on mobile?
options: Every device gets the same fixed pixel layout
The app works only in portrait
A UI that adapts to different screen sizes, orientations and densities
Images are removed on small phones
why: Phones, tablets and foldables all differ, so layouts use flexible units and constraints instead of fixed positions.

q: What is the difference between the severity and the priority of a bug?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Severity is how badly it affects the system. Priority is how soon it should be fixed
Severity is set by the customer budget and priority by the tester mood
Priority is only used for passed tests
why: A typo in the company name can be low severity but high priority. A crash in a rarely used screen can be high severity but lower priority.

q: What does this JavaScript code print?
why: Without a compare function, sort() orders items as TEXT. As text, "1" comes before "10", which comes before "9".

q: Why is this automated UI test flaky (sometimes passes, sometimes fails)?
options: A fixed sleep only guesses the waiting time. Wait explicitly until the message appears
why: If the server is slower than 500 ms the check runs too early. Explicit waits for the element make the test reliable.

q: A password field must accept 8 to 20 characters. Which lengths make the best boundary-value test?
why: Bugs hide at the edges. Test just outside and just inside each limit: 7 (too short), 8 (ok), 20 (ok), 21 (too long).

q: What is regression testing?
options: Re-running tests after a change to check that the old features still work
Testing code before it is written
Measuring how fast the app loads
why: New changes can accidentally break existing features. Regression tests catch that.

q: What does the test pyramid recommend?
options: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few slow end-to-end UI tests
Equal numbers of every kind of test
why: Small tests are fast and pinpoint problems. Big UI tests are slow and fragile, so keep them few.

q: You found a bug but cannot reproduce it a second time. What should you do?
options: Ignore it. It was a one-time glitch
Tell the developer it is their fault
Report it with everything you know (steps tried, environment, logs, screenshots) and mark it as intermittent
why: Intermittent bugs are real. Good evidence lets someone else spot the pattern later.

q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
options: Verification asks "are we building the product right?" (matches the spec). Validation asks "are we building the right product?" (meets user needs)
Verification is done only by users and validation only by developers
why: A product can match its spec perfectly and still not solve the user problem. You need both.

q: What does this JavaScript code print?
why: Decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a small tolerance.

q: What makes a good bug report?
options: A clear title, exact steps to reproduce, expected vs actual result and the environment
"It does not work" with a screenshot of the desktop
A long story about the developer
Only the tester opinion of the severity
why: The developer should be able to repeat your steps and see the same problem without asking questions.

q: The release is tomorrow and you cannot test everything. How do you choose what to test first?
options: Risk-based: test the most critical and most recently changed features first
why: When time is short, put effort where a failure would hurt most and where bugs are most likely.

q: These tests pass alone, but the second one fails when the first is skipped. What is the cause?
options: let cannot be used in tests
The tests share state and depend on their order. Each test should set up its own data
why: Independent tests can run in any order, in parallel, and one failure does not cause others.

q: What is SQL injection?
options: A way to speed up SQL queries
An attacker puts SQL code into an input so the database runs commands it should not
why: If user input is joined into a query as text, it can change the meaning of the query.

q: What does this browser JavaScript print?
why: textContent treats the value as plain text, so the browser escapes < and >. This is why textContent is safe against XSS.

q: What is the vulnerability here, and what is the standard fix?
code: String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'";
options: Buffer overflow. Use a bigger string
SQL injection. Use a PreparedStatement with parameters
why: Parameters keep data separate from the SQL command, so input can never change the query.

q: You get an email: "Your bank account is locked. Click this link and enter your password." What should you do?
options: Do not click. It is probably phishing. Open the bank website yourself or call the bank
Forward it to all your friends
Reply with your password so they can verify you
why: Phishing creates panic to make you act quickly. Always go to the real site on your own.

q: What is the best way to store user passwords?
options: In plain text so you can email them back
As a salted hash made with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2
Encrypted with a key stored in the same table
As a fast MD5 hash without a salt
why: Hashing is one-way, the salt makes every hash unique, and a slow algorithm makes guessing expensive for attackers.

q: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)?
options: Injecting malicious script into a page that other users then run in their browser
why: The attacker script runs with the same rights as the real page, so it can steal sessions or change the page.

q: What does HTTPS (TLS) protect against?
options: Someone on the network reading or changing the data between the browser and the server
A user choosing a weak password
why: HTTPS encrypts data in transit. It does not fix flaws inside the application itself.

q: What is multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
options: Requiring two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from your phone
why: Even if a password leaks, the attacker still needs the second factor.

q: A website shows another user's order when you change /orders/101 to /orders/102 in the address. What is this flaw?
options: Broken access control (IDOR). The server must check that the user owns that record
why: Hiding links is not security. Every request must be checked against the logged-in user on the server.

q: What is the security problem in this server code?
options: console.log is not allowed on servers
Passwords are written to the logs in plain text. Never log secrets
why: Logs are often shared and stored for a long time. Anyone who can read them could read every password.

q: What does this Python code print?
options: It depends on the time of day
why: A hash function is deterministic: the same input always gives the same hash. That is why passwords need a unique salt.

q: A developer pushed an AWS secret key to a public GitHub repository. What is the right first step?
options: Revoke and rotate the key immediately, then remove it from the code
Delete the file and carry on. It is gone now
Wait and see if anyone notices
why: Bots scan GitHub within minutes. Once a key was public, assume it is stolen and replace it. Removing the file is not enough.

q: What does UX (user experience) design focus on?
options: How easy, useful and pleasant the product is to use, not only how it looks
why: UI is the look of the screens. UX is the whole experience of getting something done with them.

q:
What colour is the text of

Hello

with these CSS rules?
options: Red. The first rule always wins
Blue. A class selector is more specific than an element selector
Black. The rules cancel each other
why: When two rules match, the more specific selector wins. A class beats a plain element name.

q: Why is this button a design and accessibility problem?
options: Light grey text on white has very low contrast, so it is hard to read for many people
color cannot be set on buttons
why: Low contrast hurts people with low vision, and everyone in bright sunlight.

q: In a usability test, 4 out of 5 users cannot find the "Checkout" button. What should you do?
options: Tell users to read the manual
Ignore it. One user found it
Treat it as a design problem: make the button more visible and clearly labelled, then test again
Move it to the footer in a lighter colour
why: If most users fail at the same step, the design is at fault, not the users.

q: According to WCAG, what is the minimum contrast ratio for normal body text against its background (level AA)?
why: WCAG AA asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 for large text).

q: What is a wireframe?
options: A simple, low-detail layout sketch that shows where things go
why: Wireframes let you test structure and flow cheaply before spending time on colours and details.

q: What is the purpose of a design system?
options: Reusable components, colours and rules so the product looks and behaves consistently
why: A shared set of building blocks saves time and keeps every screen consistent.

q: What does "mobile-first" design mean?
options: Only design for phones and never for desktop
Design the desktop first and shrink it
Publish in the mobile app store first
Design the small-screen layout first, then enhance it for bigger screens
why: Starting small forces you to keep only what matters, and it is easier to add to a simple layout than to remove from a crowded one.

q: A signup form has 14 required fields and many users give up. What is the best improvement?
options: Remove or postpone non-essential fields, and split a long form into clear steps
Add more fields so the data is complete
why: Every extra field costs you users. Ask only for what you really need now.

q: What does Fitts's Law say?
options: People scan pages in an F-shape
Bigger and closer targets are faster and easier to hit, so make important buttons large and easy to reach
why: It is why primary buttons are large and why thumb-friendly zones matter on phones.

q: Which error message is the most helpful for a user?
options: "Password must be at least 8 characters. Add 2 more."
why: A good error message says what happened and how to fix it, in plain words.

q: Why is this a problem for accessibility?
options: PNG files cannot be used on the web
It has no alt text, so screen reader users get no description of the image
src must be written in capital letters
why: The alt attribute describes the image for screen readers and shows when the image fails to load.
